We ran forged-JWT attack tests on our own app and closed cross-tenant vulnerabilities before they could be exploited.

Building UMKM Unggul Indonesia taught me one thing: speed comes from AI, but quality comes from guardrails.

What we put in place:
1. Tenant Isolation: Row-level security across all tables, verified with forged-JWT tests.
2. Access Control: Granular permissions + segregation of duties (nobody can approve their own void, refund, or price change).

4 practices I’m keeping for every build:
- Staged database migrations
- Atomic transactions & hash-chained audit logs
- Privacy by design 
- Hardened operations 

See the live product: www.umkmunggul.id
Case studies & full portfolio: www.aziztaufiqurrahman.com

On 27 October 2007, around 500 bloggers from across Indonesia met at Blitz Megaplex, Grand Indonesia, Jakarta, for Pesta Blogger 2007, the country's first national blogger gathering. The theme was "Suara Baru Indonesia" (A New Voice of Indonesia). Organizing chair Enda Nasution proposed making the day National Bloggers' Day, and Communications Minister Muhammad Nuh declared it on stage.

Why it still matters to me: a lot of what we now call content, online communities and personal branding grew out of those personal blogs. Communities from Makassar, Semarang, Bandung, Padang and other cities that knew each other only through comment sections finally met in person. Writing consistently and honestly built trust long before social media algorithms existed.

My lesson: having your own place on the web to write and share is still worth it, especially for developers and business owners. Platforms change, but the writing and relationships you build stay yours. Does anyone here still blog regularly?

posts.text:
I asked my AI for a new feature.
The most useful thing it asked back wasn't how to build it.
It was "what if the user already left the page when the error comes back?"

And it doesn't just ask. It comes with options:
👉 Show nothing, they've moved on
👉 Show it on the next page
👉 Save it for later

I choose one.
Then the AI writes it down as the intent, writes the proof, and builds.

This is what shipping frontend features with AI looks like for me at DANA Indonesia now.

----
How does it know what to ask?

Every feature we've built comes with its intent: plain sentences about what must stay true. Together they're a list of every promise the product makes. That's the intent corner of the triangle of truth from my last post.

So when I ask for something new, the AI doesn't start from a blank page. It reads those promises first, and asks only where my request leaves a gap or could break one of them.

It doesn't ask what colour the button should be. That's already in the design.
It doesn't ask which library to use or where the code should go. That's already in the codebase.

----
The more intent promises we add, the better its questions get.

Frontend is full of questions like this.
What if they go back before the list loads? What if they can't afford it? These used to show up as bug reports.
Now they show up as a question with options, before any code is written.

And because the AI asks those questions, you don't need to be a frontend developer to answer them.

That's the real reason I built this. Not to help developers code faster, but so a product owner, a designer, a backend engineer or a QA tester can make a real change to a frontend with AI, and not break it.

They don't need to know every edge case. The AI asks, offers options, and recommends one. They just pick.

----
Simon Sinek says start with Why.
With AI, I start with What.
The Why stays with me as a human.
The AI sharpens myWhat, and does all the How.

posts.text:
Jakarta, Cairo, Lahore: same dollar salary dream, same next problem.

Kelvin Desman, a software engineer, wrote a guide on Medium for Indonesian developers chasing remote jobs paid in US dollars. His argument: skills are rarely the obstacle. Finding employers that hire from Indonesia and pay in dollars is. And dollar pay "holds its value even when the rupiah weakens."

I agree, and I'd add what comes after the offer letter. Four things I'd tell any developer in an emerging market:

1. Check they can pay your country. Not every payroll or contractor platform supports every country. Ask early.

2. Price the net, not the gross. Platform fees, transfer fees and the exchange spread come off the top.

3. Decide when you convert. Rent is local. Savings don't have to be. Convert what you spend.

4. Keep the paper trail. Contracts and invoices matter when your bank asks where the dollars came from.

The offer is step one. Getting paid is step two, in Jakarta, Cairo or Lahore.

Which one caught you out first: the fees, the timing or the paperwork?

Inspired by Kelvin Desman's piece on Medium, 6 Jul 2026

🚨 Fitch Warns Tighter U.S. Chip Curbs Will Slow and Reshape Asia-Pacific Data-Center Investment

Fitch Ratings warned on Thursday that Asia-Pacific data-center investment will slow and become markedly more selective as tightened U.S. semiconductor export controls squeeze operators reliant on Chinese clients and advanced American AI chips.
📌 Key Regulatory Rules & Sector Fallout: 
• November 19 Export Licensing & Nvidia Halt: Effective November 19, new U.S. rules require export licenses for covered AI chip shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Thailand, as well as overseas data centers supplying substantial compute to China-based companies. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA)—placed on downgrade watch by S&P over governance concerns a day earlier, while Moody’s flagged persistent regulatory risks despite CEO Jensen Huang’s reinstatement—has instructed manufacturing partners to halt server shipments to those four Southeast Asian nations pending compliance reviews (FT). 
• Neocloud Operators & Financing Squeeze: Fitch noted the rules will widen the divide between physical facility owners and highly leveraged neocloud providers—which depend on high GPU utilization to service debt—forcing China-exposed operators to cut prices, offer lower-tier compute, or operate aging Nvidia chips without upgrade paths. Nearly completed facilities also face revenue delays and tighter credit scrutiny from lenders verifying chip supply and customer eligibility. 
• Chinese AI Model Timelines Threatened: Reuters reported that the curbs could delay flagship model releases from China’s Z.AI and Moonshot AI, with Moonshot expecting development cycles to double to 12 months or longer if overseas compute access is severed.
💡 Market Takeaway: Washington’s expansion of AI chip licensing to Southeast Asia targets the primary offshore compute workaround for Chinese AI developers. Across APAC digital infrastructure, capital and credit will rapidly rotate away from speculative, single-tenant neocloud builds toward sovereign-compliant campuses backed by verified hyperscale demand.

Hiring someone in Indonesia from abroad? You do not always need an Employer of Record.

There are three routes:

1. Pay them directly as an independent contractor. No local entity. Fits project or part-time work. Most teams pay through Wise, Deel or Payoneer.
2. Use an EoR. The provider holds the local employment contract and carries payroll, BPJS, THR and employee income tax, then invoices you. Fits a full-time employee when you do not want a local entity.
3. Set up your own company (PT PMA). The longest setup, but it fits a larger local team and a long-term commitment.

Two things that catch people out:
If a "contractor" relationship really works like employment, there is a misclassification risk.
Under Indonesian law the creator keeps rights to the work by default, so put an explicit IP-assignment clause in the contract.

posts.text:
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐡 𝐨𝐟 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐬 

Thousands of years back, the small island of Melos wanted to stay out of the war between Athens and Sparta.Athens demanded that Melos takes a side and  accept its rule.

 Thucydides captured this beautifully in his quote 

“The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.”

How true still !!

Look at the chart and here are seven insights you can comment on or save.

1. AI could become hypernational.

Early movers like US have strong position and leverage. They have got their models into products and services before alternatives could mature. This is great strategy to have and their Closed models give providers control over access. Chip export controls can make alternatives harder to build. A US rule effective 19 November 2026 requires licences for certain advanced AI chips destined for Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. This destination-based requirement has an exclusion for recipients headquartered in the US or whose ultimate parent is headquartered there, subject to reporting requirements. Two neighbouring data centres could face different requirements and treatment if one qualifies for that exclusion. Long term I do see monopoly and Competition law shaping up and attempting to level the field but that will take time.

2. China also has a game.

More competition between models can strengthen the cloud providers. Microsoft added China’s DeepSeek-R1 to Azure AI Foundry & AWS made it deployable through SageMaker JumpStart. An engineering team can try another model for writing test code or tracing bugs without moving its infrastructure. The team gets another option. The cloud provider gets another reason for the team to stay. Open-weight models will stay attractive in the long run.

3. India can play the balancing role.

India has no separate slice in this chart, but its scale and linguistic diversity make it an important market for AI. India needs models of its own and room to work with the rest of the world. Homegrown models from developers like Sarvam give India a way to invest in languages and public services that global providers may give lower priority. Jugalbandi shows the value of staying open. It combined language tools from India’s AI4Bharat with Microsoft’s Azure OpenAI Service to help villagers find government schemes through WhatsApp.

4. Hardware Punch.

A small slice can conceal industrial power. South Korea accounts for 2.3% of the models shown. Its SK hynix has a multiyear partnership with NVIDIA to develop memory for AI systems. South Korea’s position looks different when you trace who supplies the hardware leading developers depend on.

5. Multi feature Run

One model can support many features. GPT‑4 powered both role play and answer explanations in Duolingo Max at launch. That is one model behind two features in a paid product. A map of dependence would show how many products would need reworking if a widely used model went offline.

6. Global South

A large user base can attract investment while model decisions stay abroad. The World Bank found that middle income countries accounted for about half of ChatGPT’s global traffic within six months of launch. In August 2026, OpenAI reported that Brazil was one of ChatGPT’s three largest markets by weekly active users, sending about 215 million messages a day, and announced the launch of commercial operations there. OpenAI’s decision earlier that year to retire GPT‑4o from ChatGPT illustrates where control still sits. OpenAI said at the time that GPT‑4o would remain available through its API. User demand can bring a company to São Paulo. The company still decides which model people can use when they log in.

7. Specifications

A benchmark can silently become industrial policy. Google Research’s IndicGenBench evaluates models across 29 Indic languages and 13 scripts. If major buyers put tests like these into tenders, developers have a business reason to improve performance in languages that general benchmarks may overlook. What earns the contract shapes what gets built.

Risks :

The risk is that essential services come to rely on models their institutions have limited capacity to test, adapt or replace. A provider’s decision abroad can then affect whether someone gets help at home.

The response is to pool purchasing where needs overlap, test models in the languages people actually use and give smaller models with open weights a fair trial. Before signing a long contract, run the service on a second model and see what breaks.

I would like to see a map of who can still change their mind after they buy.

Chart source : Visual Capitalist, “The Countries Developing the World’s AI Models”, based on World Bank analysis of Epoch AI data.

"Nvidia has told its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers to four south-east Asian countries, as the US steps up export controls to prevent Chinese access to AI computing power.

Manufacturing partners such as Dell and Supermicro, which package Nvidia’s chips into servers, have told buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that Nvidia will not allow their orders to be shipped, according to three people with knowledge of the matter.

It is unclear whether the halt is temporary, as Nvidia and its partners try to work out how to comply with Washington’s new export controls, the people said.

The four south-east Asian countries have become favoured destinations for Chinese AI developers seeking to access Nvidia’s most advanced chips, whose exports are restricted by Washington.

The region is lucrative for Nvidia. The chipmaker booked $104bn of revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, a 72 per cent increase in 12 months, according to company accounts. Nvidia also records some of its Taiwan and China revenue via its Singapore unit.

Many Chinese groups get around US export controls by renting access through cloud computing providers that buy servers containing Nvidia chips.
...
Demand from Chinese tech companies has fuelled south-east Asia’s data centre boom, particularly in Malaysia and Indonesia, where billions of dollars have poured into the construction of AI infrastructure. The new US restrictions have put much of that investment in jeopardy.

Among those affected is Aolani, a Singapore-based cloud company that planned to provide advanced computing power to ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, through leasing agreements, said two of the people.

The disruption has led some bankers who previously agreed to finance the project to stop issuing credit worth about $500mn and to ByteDance potentially dropping the deal.

Nvidia declined to comment. Dell, Supermicro, ByteDance and Aolani did not respond to requests for comment."

Why Global Data Center Developers Fail to Secure Land in West Java and Batam: The Fatal Mistake of Selecting Sites Without 150 kV Substation Capacity

As hyperscale cloud and AI operators accelerate expansion across Greater Jakarta, West Java (Bekasi, Cikarang, Karawang, and Purwakarta), and Batam, many international sponsors approach site selection through a traditional industrial real estate lens—prioritizing land price per square meter, highway access, and proximity to submarine cable landings.

Yet in Indonesia’s high-density power corridors, buying land before underwriting high-voltage (150 kV) substation headroom and transmission evacuation capacity is the single fastest path to stranded capital. 

Developing a 50–150+ MW AI campus requires dedicated high-voltage bay allocations, multi-year transformer lead times, and strict N-1/N-2 redundancy that local 20 kV distribution feeders simply cannot support.

From an energy investment origination and enterprise risk governance perspective, Indonesian data center land acquisitions achieve institutional financial close only when verified substation capacity, binding PLN Power Supply Agreements (PSAs), and clear transmission right-of-way (ROW) corridors are validated upfront.

Six core pillars define institutional origination for bankable powered-land selection in West Java and Batam:

 1. Substation Bay Headroom & Upstream Grid-Impact Verification: Confirming physical bay availability and transformer capacity at adjacent 150 kV (or 275 kV) substations—validated against PLN’s regional RUPTL grid expansion plan—prevents multi-year connection queues.

 2. Binding Phased Power Supply Agreements (PSAs) & Ramp-Up Schedules: Locking in contractual MW delivery milestones and connection-fee (BP/UJL) terms aligned with server-hall commissioning schedules protects project IRR.

 3. Dual-Feed Transmission Redundancy & Right-of-Way (ROW) Security: Securing diverse, unencumbered underground or overhead transmission corridors from two independent substations satisfies Uptime Tier III/IV and hyperscale resilience mandates.

 4. Integrated Spatial Zoning (KKPR), Flood & Water-Supply Underwriting: Verifying industrial zoning alignment, 100-year flood elevation defenses, and closed-loop water availability alongside power capacity eliminates sequential permitting roadblocks.

 5. 24/7 Clean-Energy & Behind-the-Meter BESS Integration Readiness: Assessing proximity to solar-BESS, geothermal, or Wilayah Usaha clean-power pathways ensures future compliance with global hyperscalers’ Scope 2 and 24/7 Carbon-Free Energy targets.

 6. Clean HGB Title Chain & Zero-Tolerance ABAC Controls: Conducting forensic land-title due diligence free of overlapping claims, paired with uncompromising anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABAC) governance across utility and zoning workflows, protects institutional credit committees.

Nvidia pauses AI server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia: what it means for regional AI buildouts
On 26 November 2026, the Financial Times and The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia had instructed manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, to suspend shipments of servers containing its AI chips to four Southeast Asian markets. Partners have told customers that Nvidia will not authorise their orders. The duration is unspecified.
Context
•	The move follows a new US export rule that took effect this month requiring licences for advanced chips sent to these countries.
•	The four markets had become destinations for Chinese AI developers seeking access to restricted chips, according to reports.
•	Per the WSJ, Nvidia is assessing whether regional partners meet US export requirements.
•	It comes days after the US Commerce Department added Megaspeed and Alibaba's Singapore unit to its Entity List.
Implications for businesses
1.	Timelines: AI data centre and cloud projects in the region may face delays.
2.	Due diligence: expect tighter end-user checks, licence requests and documentation from suppliers.
3.	Costs: constrained supply could raise prices for compute in the region.
4.	Policy watch: the balance between preventing chip diversion and supporting legitimate regional growth will be closely negotiated.
Supporters see stricter controls as necessary to stop restricted chips reaching China. Critics argue broad pauses penalise legitimate customers and fast-growing regional markets.
If you're building on AI infrastructure in Southeast Asia, how are you planning around this?
#Nvidia #ExportControls #AIInfrastructure #DataCentres #SoutheastAsia #SupplyChain

China's AI development is facing mounting challenges as US chip restrictions tighten and  
 
American AI companies strengthen their safeguards against unauthorized model distillation.

NVIDIA has instructed manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia, according to media reports. 
 
The US regulations, effective November 19, introduce licensing requirements for certain advanced chip exports and remote computing arrangements. 
 
Overseas data centers are estimated to provide approximately 24% of China's AI computing power.

Z.AI's 3-trillion-parameter GLM-5.5 could be delayed until early 2027 or later, while Moonshot AI's Kimi K4 could arrive around mid-2027. 
 
Moonshot's development cycles could double from six months to a year or longer if overseas computing access is completely cut off. 
 
Meanwhile, OpenAI and Anthropic are strengthening defenses against unauthorized model distillation, which allows developers to train competitive AI models at lower costs. 
 
Anthropic identified nearly 200 million exchanges with Claude linked to suspected distillation campaigns involving several Chinese developers. 
 
Moonshot has previously maintained that its Kimi K3 performance improvements resulted from original architectural changes. 
 
Together, these developments threaten the cost advantages that have helped Chinese AI companies compete with their American counterparts. 
 
Content Source: TechCrunch, Reuters, US Department of Commerce, Anthropic 
 
Media Source: NVIDIA, Asia Financial

Nvidia has just stopped shipping AI servers to four countries. Not because of demand — because of Washington.
The Financial Times reported on Thursday that Nvidia told manufacturing partners Dell and Supermicro to halt server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. The move follows new US export controls that took effect on 19 November, requiring licences for advanced chips sent to those countries — and Brazil.
The target is not really Southeast Asia. It is the workaround: Chinese AI developers who could not buy Nvidia's most advanced chips directly have been renting computing power from data centres in the region instead. The new rules close that route, and cloud providers now have 90 days to prove their end users include no restricted entities.
It is unclear whether the halt is temporary while Nvidia and its partners work out compliance. Nvidia declined to comment. But the disruption is already spreading: Bloomberg reports a loan of about $480 million sought by Singapore cloud provider Aolani to buy Nvidia GPUs has been put on hold.
Here is the bigger picture. The AI race is no longer decided only in labs and fabs. It is decided in export-control rules, licence queues and loan committees — the plumbing of who gets to compute.
Chips are the new oil. And the tap now has a licence attached to it.

What Makes a Renewable Project Bankable in Southeast Asia? 

Blended finance is often described as a way to mobilise private capital for renewable energy. A report published on 28 October by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and Convergence makes the point more precisely: concessional capital is most useful when it addresses a clearly defined, project-level risk that can be mitigated. It is less effective when the main barriers are structural or regulatory.

The report examines rooftop solar, decentralised energy, offshore wind and battery storage in Indonesia, the Philippines and Viet Nam. It notes that bankability also depends on credible contracts and revenue frameworks, transparent procurement, and physical readiness such as transmission and distribution networks. Blended finance can share or absorb selected risks; it cannot substitute for these foundations.

For corporate buyers, developers and investors, the report offers a useful lens for reviewing a project proposal, not a promise of funding or a universal financing standard. Ask what specific risk the concessional capital is designed to address, who retains the remaining exposure, and what evidence supports the project’s revenue pathway. If the case depends on concessional support while major grid, policy or contractual gaps remain unresolved, those conditions deserve separate scrutiny.

The IEA recommends using concessional capital only where it adds clear value, tailoring the instrument to the constraint, and setting exit indicators as commercial viability improves. That shifts the discussion from “Is there blended finance?” to “Does this structure address the actual risk, and can support taper off?”

The report focuses on three Southeast Asian markets and does not establish Taiwan financing policy. Its distinctions between project-level risks and system-level barriers can still help readers ask more specific questions when assessing regional renewable energy pipelines.

Which risk would you want a project sponsor to explain first?

#RenewableEnergy #ProjectFinance #EnergyTransition #SoutheastAsia #EnergyInvestment

Can Indonesia turn its 100 GWp solar target into real deployed capacity by 2029? A new Ember report shows that governance reforms, not technology or cost, are the real bottleneck holding back growth.

🔹Current gap and core barriers
With only 1.5 GW of installed solar capacity at the end of 2025, Indonesia faces structural frictions across its policy framework. Administratively set ceiling tariffs fail to reflect falling solar costs, land acquisition can take up to 40 months before construction starts, corporate buyers have limited routes to procure new clean power, rooftop solar lost its export credit incentive in 2024, and standalone battery storage lacks a dedicated regulatory framework.

🔹Key reform priorities
The report proposes six targeted fixes that preserve state utility PLN’s central role in the power system:
- Replace fixed ceiling tariffs with competitive reverse auctions to enable transparent price discovery.
- Centralise land preparation with standardised leasing options to de-risk project siting and shorten development cycles.
- Introduce virtual power purchase agreements (VPPAs) to unlock up to 12 GW of new solar capacity driven by corporate demand.
- Reinstate fair net billing for rooftop solar with grid safeguards, estimated to save the state IDR 1.9 trillion by 2030.
- Establish a clear remuneration framework for battery storage to support grid flexibility and firm solar supply.
- Streamline procurement through a dedicated agency working alongside PLN to standardise contracts and tender processes.

SNEC's Insights
1️⃣ For emerging solar markets, administrative efficiency and policy predictability matter more than raw resource potential. Governance bottlenecks typically slow deployment long before technology or cost become limiting factors.
2️⃣ VPPAs are a pragmatic middle path for markets without full power sector liberalisation. They channel corporate decarbonisation capital into new solar capacity while preserving utility revenue and grid control.
3️⃣ Pre-cleared, tender-ready sites are a high-impact, low-profile lever. Resolving land and grid access before auctions reduces developer risk far more effectively than incremental tariff incentives.

🔹Bottom line: 
The upcoming revision of Indonesia’s national electricity plan is a critical window to align regulation with its 100 GWp ambition. With targeted governance reforms, solar can become a core pillar of Indonesia’s energy security, industrial competitiveness and decarbonisation.

AI Data Centre Investments: Time to De-Risk the Technology Strategy

Recent US regulatory developments affecting AI server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia raise an important question:

Are our AI data-centre investments too dependent on a single technology ecosystem?

Disruptions are not new to infrastructure development. What matters is how effectively we anticipate risks, mitigate their impact and institutionalise lessons learned throughout the project development and execution lifecycle. 

Every challenge should strengthen our next investment decision, project strategy and delivery model.

The opportunity is to rethink risk before it becomes a project-delivery or financial challenge.

Three strategic priorities:

🔹 Diversify: Explore alternative OEMs and compute platforms AMD, Intel, Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro.

🔹 Design for Flexibility: Build technology-agnostic infrastructure capable of accommodating evolving AI hardware.

🔹 Protect Investments: Secure supply chains, power, cooling capacity and regulatory compliance from day one.

To developers and investors:

Don’t build multi-billion-dollar AI infrastructure investments around a single hardware supplier.

Build flexibility into design. Diversify technology partnerships. Stress-test investment assumptions. Protect project timelines and returns.

The next competitive advantage may not simply be access to the latest GPU it may be the ability to deploy reliable, compliant and scalable compute infrastructure regardless of the hardware ecosystem.

Build for flexibility. Invest for resilience. Stay ahead of disruption.

I asked my AI for a new feature.
The most useful thing it asked back wasn't how to build it.
It was "what if the user already left the page when the error comes back?"

And it doesn't just ask. It comes with options:
👉 Show nothing, they've moved on
👉 Show it on the next page
👉 Save it for later

I choose one.
Then the AI writes it down as the intent, writes the proof, and builds.

This is what shipping frontend features with AI looks like for me at DANA Indonesia now.

----
How does it know what to ask?

Every feature we've built comes with its intent: plain sentences about what must stay true. Together they're a list of every promise the product makes. That's the intent corner of the triangle of truth from my last post.

So when I ask for something new, the AI doesn't start from a blank page. It reads those promises first, and asks only where my request leaves a gap or could break one of them.

It doesn't ask what colour the button should be. That's already in the design.
It doesn't ask which library to use or where the code should go. That's already in the codebase.

----
The more intent promises we add, the better its questions get.

Frontend is full of questions like this.
What if they go back before the list loads? What if they can't afford it? These used to show up as bug reports.
Now they show up as a question with options, before any code is written.

And because the AI asks those questions, you don't need to be a frontend developer to answer them.

That's the real reason I built this. Not to help developers code faster, but so a product owner, a designer, a backend engineer or a QA tester can make a real change to a frontend with AI, and not break it.

They don't need to know every edge case. The AI asks, offers options, and recommends one. They just pick.

----
Simon Sinek says start with Why.
With AI, I start with What.
The Why stays with me as a human.
The AI sharpens myWhat, and does all the How.

Jakarta, Cairo, Lahore: same dollar salary dream, same next problem.

Kelvin Desman, a software engineer, wrote a guide on Medium for Indonesian developers chasing remote jobs paid in US dollars. His argument: skills are rarely the obstacle. Finding employers that hire from Indonesia and pay in dollars is. And dollar pay "holds its value even when the rupiah weakens."

I agree, and I'd add what comes after the offer letter. Four things I'd tell any developer in an emerging market:

1. Check they can pay your country. Not every payroll or contractor platform supports every country. Ask early.

2. Price the net, not the gross. Platform fees, transfer fees and the exchange spread come off the top.

3. Decide when you convert. Rent is local. Savings don't have to be. Convert what you spend.

4. Keep the paper trail. Contracts and invoices matter when your bank asks where the dollars came from.

The offer is step one. Getting paid is step two, in Jakarta, Cairo or Lahore.

Which one caught you out first: the fees, the timing or the paperwork?

Inspired by Kelvin Desman's piece on Medium, 6 Jul 2026

#Greece /#Harvest ‘We come back to save our parents’ livelihood. ’With price of olive oil sinking and difficulty of finding workers, some Greeks take time off from their jobs to participate in harvest -Kathimerini

Every morning, October-December, a familiar routine unfolds in olive-growing regions: fields fill with workers, & nets are spread out to ensure not a single olive is lost, while the rhythmic clatter of harvesting poles & long sticks sets the pace. In the afternoon, pickup trucks & tractors, laden with cargo, transport sacks of olives to mills.

This year in particular, with olive oil prices hitting record lows & difficulty of finding labor remaining a persistent headache (even when workers can be found, daily wages range from 70-€100), young people with roots in these rural areas are not sitting idly by. They step away from their jobs & daily lives, travel to their ancestral lands, & pitch in with the harvest. A mechanical engineer takes leave from her job in London. A teacher returns from a trip to Indonesia and heads straight to the fields. A stand-up comedian schedules his performances around the conclusion of the olive harvest.

For 27-year-old Elena Malapani, the harvest season has been a constant, ingrained tradition since her primary school years. Today, Malapani is a mechanical engineer and has been living and working abroad for the past three years. However, every year she makes a point of traveling to her family’s olive groves in Kalamata, using up whatever leave she has available. The primary reason is financial.

“The price of olive oil is under three and a half euros. It’s very difficult for us. At this price, with labor costs through the roof, it simply doesn’t make economic sense to hire workers or even to own olive trees. So, as a family, we try to do more of the work ourselves,” she tells Kathimerini. Malapani had the foresight to book her flight tickets well in advance to secure a better price. “I got a round trip ticket for €120. That’s only about a day and a half’s worth of wages. It’s worth it for us,” she says, quickly doing the math in her head...

Beyond the financial aspect, the olive harvest serves as a great opportunity for her to see her loved ones and take a break from constant screen time. “Since I live abroad, I can’t always be close to my family. This way, I get to spend a good amount of time with them. At the same time, it’s liberating to set your phone aside, only picking it up during breaks, and simply disconnect from all forms of communication.”

...Yet, she notes, there is a certain paradox: “Many of us young people left Greece in search of better career opportunities and higher wages. But when harvest season arrives, we try to get time off, return home, and help our families. We go abroad to secure our own future, but we come back to Greece to save our parents’ livelihood,” Malapani says.

From One Furnace to a Multi-Year Roadmap: Strategic Fit for Heat Treatment Furnace Partners

A heat treatment furnace should be selected as a multi-year process asset, not as a one-off equipment purchase. For buyers building a smart manufacturing roadmap, the right partner is the one whose process coverage, customization range and capacity rhythm still fit three to five years out.

Start with process roadmap fit. If your plan includes carburizing, hardening, carbonitriding and tempering, the supplier should be able to explain how each furnace type and configuration supports that sequence—not only quote a single standard model. Then test ODM depth: can the partner adapt equipment size, automation level and performance targets as your parts mix and volume change? That is a continuity question, not a price-list question.

Capacity signals matter, but they should be read together. A 50-set annual output, 3–5 sets monthly and a 150-day typical lead time describe a delivery rhythm. The practical check is whether the supplier can reserve slots for your staged rollout and support installation, commissioning and later expansion without changing the process logic.

NORSEN offers one evidence set to test against: a 10-engineer R&D team, a 6,000 m² facility, 40% export share across markets including Russia, Vietnam, Indonesia and Turkey, 100% pre-shipment testing, and free remote technical assistance. These facts do not prove fit by themselves; they show what to verify in a partner's long-term support model.

The strategic-fit question is simple: can this supplier still answer your process, automation and capacity questions after the first furnace is running? That is the difference between an equipment vendor and a roadmap partner.

At the 140th Canton Fair, the best engineering decision I made for a European client was telling them NOT to buy. 🇨🇳🛑

Last month, I was on the floor in Guangzhou supporting an Italian client scouting high-end sanitaryware: faucets, shower trays, and walk-in glass enclosures.
The halls were packed with hundreds of glossy booths and aggressive pricing. Yet, when we stripped away the marketing brochures and audited the actual Bills of Materials (BOM) and technical compliance files, the picture changed completely:

1️⃣ Walk-in Shower Enclosures (Glass & Aluminum Profiles):
Under European Construction Products Regulations (CPR), you don’t just buy tempered glass—you buy a certified system backed by valid test reports and a legally binding Declaration of Performance (DoP), tightened further by regulatory updates introduced earlier this year. Out of dozens of exhibitors we screened, only one manufacturer—already supplying major European DIY retailers—had a complete, verifiable technical dossier and BOM compliance.

2️⃣ High-End Faucets & Sanitary Brassware:
European drinking-water hygiene and heavy-metal leaching standards are undergoing a major regulatory shift, with strict new rules coming into full force in 2027. While most factories were still pushing legacy alloys and outdated valve cartridges, only the top-tier OEMs are actively re-tooling for the 2027 compliance wave.
If we had bought based on booth samples and Proforma Invoice discounts, my client would have faced customs seizures, CE/DoP liability, or unsellable inventory within 12 months.

Instead, we locked in the sole compliant supplier for the walk-in enclosures—verifying every component from the aluminum extrusion profile down to the hardware BOM—and put the faucet procurement on strategic hold until the 2027-ready production lines are validated.

In global sourcing, a sales agent gets paid when you place an order. ACost & Product Engineer earns their fee when they protect your P&L from regulatory traps, flawed BOMs, and non-compliant tooling.

With 20+ years of on-the-ground experience as a Manufacturing Engineer and Zhongguotong bridging European/North American engineering standards with Asian manufacturing (China, Vietnam, and Indonesia), I help industrial companies and hardware innovators manage Cost Engineering, multi-level BOM analysis, DFM, CE/DoP technical compliance, and factory audits—turning Far East supply chains into a controlled engineering discipline.

Wrapping up an unforgettable month in Matsuyama, Japan!  🇯🇵✨

From mid-October to mid-November 2026, I had the privilege of joining the Short-Term Student Exchange Program between Universitas Gadjah Mada (UGM) and Ehime University as a research exchange student at the Concrete Laboratory.

Under the supervision of Prof. Kawaai Keiyu and alongside Bima Sukma Aji, I assisted in investigating "Red Mud and Hematite for Steel Corrosion Resistance in Concrete." Specially, we evaluated hematite, an iron-rich component associated with bauxite residue (red mud), at 5% to 20% partial cement replacement against conventional OPC, monitoring steel reinforcement corrosion behaviour through Half-Cell Potential (HCP) and Microcell Current Density (Icorr) under both non-chloride and chloride-admixed conditions.

Beyond the lab work and presenting my research poster at the final Poster Session, this exchange was truly about the people and culture. Every moment pushed me to grow both as and an aspiring structural engineer and as a global learner. My deepest gratitude to Prof. Kawaai Keiyu, Mas Bima Sukma Aji, all my friends from UGM and ITB that attended the same program whether it is the one-month program or the six-month program, Ehime University students both from Indonesia and/or Japan, colleagues at the Concrete Laboratory, and Departemen Teknik Sipil and Lingkungan (DTSL) FT UGM for making this experience possible.

Excited to bring these insights back to Yogyakarta as I continue my final year and undergraduate thesis!

Southeast Asia is about to build gigawatts of new data-centre capacity. Singapore has just given it a rulebook for liquid cooling.

At EAC Bangkok, Prof PS Lee, Head of Mechanical Engineering at National University of Singapore, presented SS 726:2026. It is Singapore's new standard for liquid cooling in tropical data centres, published by Enterprise Singapore.

It covers both single-phase direct-to-chip and single-phase immersion. It also spans the whole facility lifecycle:
🔹 equipment and materials
🔹 pre-deployment and commissioning
🔹 operations and maintenance
🔹 risk management
🔹 sustainability indicators

We think this matters well beyond Singapore. Across Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, many of the AI data centres being designed today will be liquid-cooled from day one. Until now, owners and engineers had to agree specifications project by project. A published standard for a tropical climate gives designers, operators, regulators and investors a shared reference point.

Thank you, Prof Lee, for the years of work behind this, from the Sustainable Tropical Data Centre Testbed to SS 726.

At QuettaFlow we work across both cooling routes the standard covers:
💧 Single-phase immersion: our VasEdge and VasRack systems
🔧 Single-phase direct-to-chip: rack-scale DLC projects for data-centre customers

We welcome the clarity, and we're mapping our design and commissioning documentation to the standard's lifecycle stages.

Thank you also to EAC and the Enmore team for bringing the region's engineers into one room.

Since 1945, Indonesia's GDP per capita has risen more than tenfold, and energy demand has grown alongside it, met largely by coal. Yet despite pledging 23% renewables by 2025 on the road to Net Zero 2060, Indonesia reached only a 13% renewable share.
The bottleneck isn't simply geography or weak foreign climate finance. It is a domestic failure to build an economically efficient electricity market.

In Indonesia's vertically integrated single-buyer system, the state utility (PLN) is locked in by frozen retail tariffs, 20- to 30-year IPP contracts, and an artificially suppressed $70/tonne coal price cap under the Domestic Market Obligation (DMO). As long as coal is implicitly subsidized through below-market prices, solar and wind are economically pushed out before they can compete on merit.

In the attached note, I explore whether replacing the DMO price cap with a cost-neutral Domestic Tax Obligation (DTO) could restore a competitive electricity market. The idea is to let coal reflect its real market value while recycling windfall tax revenue through the Ministry of Finance and Indonesia's National Single Social and Economic Data (DTSEN) to protect lower-income households. I also look at where reform stalls across Parliament, the Ministry of Finance, and the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources, including what a Presidential Regulation can address versus what requires a formal statutory Act.

I would genuinely appreciate perspectives from energy policy analysts, power systems engineers, and researchers at institutions like the ASEAN Centre for Energy (ACE) or across the sector:
Can Indonesia's DMO realistically be reformed under the current institutional setup? And if it can, would fixing that price distortion effectively push the electricity market toward a faster, more competitive transition?

Nvidia’s suspension of server shipments to Southeast Asia signals a significant escalation in the geopolitical competition for artificial intelligence computing capacity.

The United States is expanding its semiconductor export control strategy beyond physical hardware transfers to address remote access to advanced computational infrastructure.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Nvidia has instructed manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro Computer, to temporarily suspend server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia.

The decision reportedly follows updated U.S. export regulations intended to prevent Chinese organizations from circumventing semiconductor restrictions by remotely accessing advanced AI computing resources hosted in third countries.

According to the Institute for Progress, Southeast Asian data centers have supplied an estimated 24% of China’s AI computing capacity.

This development represents a fundamental evolution in technology export controls. Regulatory oversight is increasingly shifting from the physical movement of advanced semiconductors toward the accessibility, utilization, and ultimate beneficiaries of computational resources.

For Southeast Asian economies, these restrictions could introduce considerable uncertainty surrounding hyperscale data center investments, infrastructure development, foreign investment, and emerging sovereign AI initiatives.

Cloud service providers and infrastructure operators may also face increasingly stringent requirements involving customer verification, workload monitoring, access management, and regulatory compliance.

The duration of Nvidia’s shipment suspension remains unspecified.

Key Takeaways: Advanced computational capacity is increasingly being treated as a strategic national security resource. Traditional semiconductor export controls are expanding toward governance of remotely accessible computing infrastructure and its ultimate users.

Implications: Semiconductor manufacturers, hyperscale operators, governments, and institutional investors must increasingly incorporate geopolitical exposure into infrastructure planning and technology procurement. Sovereign AI capabilities, geographically diversified computing architectures, and independently governed infrastructure could become increasingly valuable. The geopolitical competition for AI supremacy is evolving beyond control of semiconductor manufacturing toward control of the global computational ecosystem itself.

Can You Really Teach an Old Dog New Tricks? 🦴✨
OK, so I’m not especially old… but I’m certainly no spring chicken! 🐥
If you’ve ever looked at my profile, you’ll have seen that I’ve worked with some pretty cool companies over the years. I’m pleased to say I’ve remained great friends with them all.
For the past 10 years, I’ve largely worked on a consultancy basis, supporting not only those companies but others as far afield as the USA and Indonesia.
I started in the Royal Navy, moved into HVAC design, spent around three years as a Second Engineer at a large ammonia refrigeration plant and then entered the world of international business development for manufacturing companies almost 30 years ago.
I’ve formally studied Marine Engineering, Building Services Engineering, Refrigeration Engineering, Marketing and ILM Management.
And apparently, I’m still not finished learning!
A while ago I spent some time working with a well-established manufacturing company with significant growth ambitions. The senior management team had been there for 20+ years, they were genuinely nice people with great knowledge of their business and products…. And they way they have always done things!
But I’ve always believed that if you want to move forward and grow significantly, you also need to look back at what you’ve been doing.
There will be some fantastic things worth preserving… but probably a few things that could be done way better and certainly new ways of doing things 🎇
One saying has always stuck with me:
“If you keep doing the same things, you can only expect the same results.”
The company had an impressive, all-singing-and-dancing CRM system. I can only imagine what it had cost them!£$
Yet it was being used nowhere near its full potential, I extracted the data and found around 900 contacts, of which approximately 600 were suppliers.
By their own admission, they really had no concept of how marketing could serve them.
No real LinkedIn strategy. No e-flyers. No reciprocal company links. And, surprisingly, a reluctance to share detailed product information.
Anyway, so what is this dogs latest trick?
I’ve been building my own industry-specific prospecting and marketing AI Agent. 🤖
Of course, there are thousands of experts out there doing this professionally, but this was something I wanted to try for myself - it’s been a real eye opener and actually quite enjoyable.
Writing the AI brief requires considerable thought, industry knowledge and a clear understanding of what you want to achieve. But once you get started, you can continually adapt it, feed in new information and refine the way it works.
At the end of my engagement, I left the company with a much stronger foundation for future sales and marketing activity, including:
• Multiple prospect databases organised by customers, locations and opportunities
• Verified contacts, email addresses and LinkedIn profiles
• Customer-published sustainability commitments
• A structured marketing planner and LinkedIn post templates
• A significantly improved company presence and shop window
And, importantly, a prospecting database containingthousands of relevant contacts rather than a CRM largely populated by suppliers.
This is, of course, only the beginning.
I call it“casting the wide net” — identifying opportunities, building relationships and creating the foundations for meaningful sales growth.
I’m not one of those flashy, self-proclaimed “Business Transformation Specialists”.
I’m simply someone who’s learned a few things along the way:
• Doing the same thing repeatedly will often deliver the same results… or worse.
• Never stop learning. Keep an open mind, listen to those around you and be prepared to challenge established ways of working.
• Recognising what isn’t working is just as important as celebrating what is.
So, can you teach an old dog new tricks?
I think you can. And sometimes, those new tricks can make quite a difference.
I currently have some spare consultancy capacity until around the end of February, EHC Consulting.
You might find that this old-school BD guy still has a few new tricks up his sleeve! 👍

EMPOWERMENT WITHOUT LOSING CONTROL: BUILDING A HIGH-PERFORMING PROJECT ORGANIZATION IN CHINA

In 2018, I was assigned to Shanghai for several years to help establish a global Gasification Project Delivery Organization.

We started with the acquisition of established gasification technologies. And a core team of around 20 people which we quickly grew to 300, combining experienced Chinese employees from the existing air separation project delivery organization with talented engineers recruited from China's established gasification industry. Our initial project was a $650m coal gasification project in Inner Mongolia. But the organization grew rapidly. Within nine months, we were executing several other coal gasification projects across China.

In parallel, under my leadership, we were developing a presence in Indonesia and working to establish the foundations for a coal gasification industry there. This included executing a $70m FEED for a separate proposed $2.5bn coal-to-methanol project.

A central part of my leadership approach was empowerment, supported by effective governance.

I believe in giving capable teams the freedom to deliver in the way they know best, without unnecessary interference in operational detail. The role of leadership is to provide direction, establish clear accountability and maintain appropriate oversight through regular reviews and stage gates.

The results were impressive. The Chinese team developed real ownership, confidence and pride in their work. This was particularly evident on the Inner Mongolia project during the pandemic, when severe restrictions made project execution exceptionally challenging. The team's resilience and determination to keep the project moving forward over such a prolonged period remain among my strongest memories.

Empowerment also meant creating opportunities for talented people to grow. We gave ambitious engineers stretch assignments, including leadership of functional teams, helping develop the next generation of project leaders.

My own contribution was not limited to strategic oversight. I identified weaknesses in project reporting and worked directly with the team to improve its clarity, consistency and credibility. The resulting templates were subsequently adopted across the wider China organization, strengthening confidence among senior executives in the US.

My conclusion: Effective project governance is not about controlling every detail. It is about creating the conditions in which capable people can take ownership, make decisions and deliver—while maintaining the transparency and oversight that give senior leadership confidence.

Getting that balance right can make a significant difference to project performance.

How do you strike the right balance between empowering project teams and maintaining effective governance?

Fixing a problem usually takes minutes.
Finding the root cause can take hours.

I'm a Technical Support Associate. When an issue hits, my job is to stop the bleeding as fast as possible.

But before we can stop it, we have to find the root cause.

That means:
• Opening 4–10 dashboards
• Checking service after service
• Asking team after team

And every team says the same thing: "Not on our side."

They're right. The root cause is hiding between them.

I'm not an AI engineer by title. I started with small Python scripts to automate the boring parts of my shift. Then I learned to build AI agents, and one question wouldn't leave me alone:

What if we could see everything from above? 🚁

That question became Revive, an AI agent that works like a helicopter view. You ask it one question, it looks across every service at once, and shows you where the root cause really is.

📈 Five weeks in:
→ 4–10 places to check became 1 question
→ Minutes of analysis became seconds
→ Used every single day, weekends included

What I learned along the way: you don't need the perfect title to build with AI. Start from the problem that frustrates you most. And the goal was never to replace anyone. It was to give everyone the full picture.

🙏 Grateful to be building this at DANA Indonesia. Thank you Mas Hafiz Dzulfikar, Frico Simon andKhairani Malau for building and shaping it together, and PakZikry Zakiyulfuadi, Pak Amir Rachman PakKrisna Prihasto, Mas mikail amrullah for your guidance along the way.

Karatau madang di hulu,
babuah babungo balun.
Marantau bujang dahulu,
di rumah baguno balun.

An old Minangkabau pantun: go out into the world first, young man, because at home you are of no use yet.

For centuries, Minang men from West Sumatra have left their villages on merantau to seek wealth, knowledge and experience, and to come back better than they left. 

That tradition shaped Hatta, Agus Salim, Hamka and countless others.
It also shaped me.

I grew up in Padang, raised by my mother, in a house just 10 metres from the shoreline. 

Every morning I watched the fishermen come back from their night at sea, pulling their boats onto the sand with whatever the ocean had given them. Without knowing it, I was watching merantau in miniature: go out into the dark, work hard, and come home with something to share.

My mum can speak English and Dutch. Fluently. I learned English watching Scooby-Doo and Little House on the Prairie while she watched me practice. Then came Jakarta for university, and after that 35+ years in Oil & Gas across Indonesia, Singapore, the UAE, the US, Saudi Arabia and the UK.

One principle has stayed with me the whole way: "Alam takambang jadi guru", the wide world is your teacher.

But the rantau is only half of the story. 

As the Minang saying goes:

"Satinggi-tinggi tabang bangau,
baliaknyo ka kubangan juo."

However high the heron flies, it always returns to the pond it came from. 
Like those fishermen, we go out so that we can bring something back.

To every young engineer wondering whether to take the leap abroad: the rantau is waiting. 

Go, learn, and come home with your catch.

Pulau Pandan jauh di tengah,
di balik Pulau Angso Duo.
Hancua badan dikanduang tanah,
budi baiak dikana juo.

(The body returns to the earth, but good deeds are remembered.)

#Merantau #Minangkabau #Engineering #OilAndGas #CareerJourney

posts.text:
Two electric aircraft. Each around 10 tonnes. Both flew this year.
The short-haul regional cockpit is about to change.
✈️ On 14 November, COMAC's CE-25A made its first piloted flight in Binzhou, China.
19 seats.
10 electrically driven ducted fans along the wing.
Two pilots and a flight-test engineer on board.
16 minutes 38 seconds. 60.4 km.

✈️ In August, Heart Aerospace's X1 flew from Plattsburgh, New York.
Over 11 tonnes.
Four electric motors producing more than 1 MW.
27 minutes in the air.
A full-scale demonstrator for the 30-seat ES-30, targeted for service in 2031.

Why this matters:
These aren't small two-seat trainers.
They're approaching the size of real regional aircraft — the kind that connect small towns and islands.
And neither was built alone.
COMAC partnered with battery maker CATL and Shanghai Jiao Tong University.
Heart Aerospace was founded in Sweden, now builds in the US, and is backed by airlines and investors across borders.
I flew the Cessna 208B on short charter and cargo routes in Indonesia.
Those are exactly the sectors where electric aircraft could make their first real impact.

📚 Where to learn more:
• NASA Technical Reports Server (ntrs.nasa.gov) — search "electrified aircraft propulsion" for free research papers
• EASA Special Condition SC E-19 (easa.europa.eu) — how regulators approach certifying electric and hybrid propulsion

Question for pilots, engineers and planners:
Battery weight still limits range.
So where does electric flight win first — island-hopping, regional cargo, or flight training?
And what would it take for DGCA to certify one for Indian skies? 👇
Sources: 
Gulf News – Heart's X1 and China's piloted 19-seater
EASA – Final Special Condition SC E-19, Electric/Hybrid Propulsion System
EASA – SC E-19 Issue 1 (PDF)
#ElectricAviation #RegionalAviation #SustainableAviation #AviationTechnology #FutureOfFlight

Four out of five private dollars in Southeast Asian tech now go to one kind of company.

The e-Conomy SEA 2026 report by Google, Temasek and Bain is titled "Building the intelligent economy". Its Bain analysis found that AI-focused companies captured about 80% of private funding in the region.

Why this matters for hiring:

Funding is a leading signal. When money moves to AI-focused companies, the teams around that work grow too. Not only machine learning engineers, but the people who make AI useful inside a business:

- Data engineers who keep the pipelines clean
- Cloud and DevOps engineers who run the infrastructure
- Business analysts who turn a use case into requirements
- Pre-sales and customer success people who explain the product to buyers

For hiring managers in Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand, it means competing for these profiles with well-funded teams. Clear role design and a fast, respectful process count for more than ever.

For IT professionals, it means skills that sit next to AI are worth building now, even if your title doesn't have "AI" in it.

At Base Camp we recruit across IT, go-to-market and corporate roles in Asia, and we see this shift in the briefs we receive.

Which role in your team has changed the most because of AI this year?

🤖 Swiss Future Week at Politeknik Industri ATMI

On 11 November 2026, Politeknik Industri ATMI Cikarang welcomed students from three participating schools — SDK Penabur Kota Jababeka, SD Pangudi Luhur Bernadus Kota Deltamas, and SD Santo Leo III — for an interactive introduction to vocational and technical education. The visit was attended by Mathias Domenig (Deputy Head of Mission) from the Embassy of Switzerland and Olivia Nathalie Noor (Executive Director) representing SwissCham Indonesia, highlighting the longstanding connection between Swiss expertise and Indonesia's vocational education ecosystem. Founded in 1968, ATMI has built its educational approach around practical learning, technical competence, and industry relevance.
 
Students took part in a guided campus tour, exploring the ATMI Recycle Studio, manufacturing workshop, and mechatronics workshop to learn about plastic recycling, manufacturing processes, workplace safety, robotics, and automation. A key highlight was the hands-on line follower robot activity, where students assembled and tested their own robots before taking part in a fun competition. The program also featured student and graduate stories, an open Q&A session, and opportunities to discover different technical study programs and career pathways.
 
By combining practical experience with exposure to real learning environments, ATMI demonstrated how early engagement with technical education can spark curiosity and inspire future engineers. SwissCham Indonesia extends its appreciation to Politeknik Industri ATMI Cikarang and the Embassy of Switzerland in Indonesia for supporting this initiative and helping strengthen connections between education and industry.

posts.text:
Wednesday taught the AI industry a lesson in one morning.

The Nasdaq fell 4.6%. Nvidia fell more than 9%. Anthropic touched $73.85 — 11% below its $83 IPO price.

By the close, almost all of it came back. The Nasdaq finished down just 0.6%. Nvidia closed at $149.30, down 3.9%. Anthropic closed at $82.79, up 1% — still below its IPO price.
Then, on Thursday, the harder news arrived. The Financial Times reported that Nvidia has told Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping AI servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, after new US export rules took effect on 19 November. It is not clear yet how long the halt lasts.
So the question is no longer only "how good is the model?"

It is also: can you get the hardware, can you prove where it will run, and can you ship a system that survives a rule changing overnight?
That is backend work. Deployment, compliance checks, audit trails, and systems that fail safely when the world changes around them.

I build those systems — Node.js, MongoDB, REST APIs, and agents that touch real inventory and real machines, with human approval where money moves.

If you are hiring a backend engineer who thinks about the whole system, not just the model, my inbox is open.

What does a mid-level software engineer in Indonesia ask for in a job post?

The median advertised salary is Rp 6.5 jt a month. The middle half of posts sit between Rp 5.0 jt and Rp 8.1 jt. That is from 63 job posts in the last 90 days that published a pay range.

Other mid-level medians from the same window:
Sales & business development: Rp 5.5 jt (144 posts)
Marketing: Rp 5.8 jt (109 posts)
Data & AI: Rp 7.3 jt (16 posts)

What these numbers are: advertised pay from job posts that show a salary range. Not offers, not payroll. Only about 1 in 5 listings show pay at all, so this is the transparent slice of the market. A role and seniority cell appears only when it has at least 5 posts.

If you are budgeting a hire in Indonesia, the full benchmark has 31 role and seniority cells with P25 to P75 ranges and an anonymized CSV download.

🔹 Sterilization — Steam treatment inactivates enzymes, halts FFA rise, loosens fruit from the bunch, and softens the mesocarp for efficient pressing.

🔹 Digestion — Precise temperature and residence-time control ruptures oil cells and prepares optimal mash consistency.
🔹 Pressing — Screw presses engineered for high extraction rate and low cake oil content.
🔹 Clarification — Multi-stage separation recovers crude palm oil (CPO) while minimizing neutral oil loss in sludge.

posts.text:
PP 33/2026 Sets a Floor, Not a Ceiling

BLUF: Compliance with Indonesia's PP 33/2026 is the floor of security, not the ceiling. The regulation mostly governs process: roles, assessments and notification. It does not, by itself, stop an attack.

With the regulation taking effect on 16 January 2027, many Jakarta enterprise security budgets are focused on compliance deliverables and standard XDR. Attackers do not read compliance binders. They exploit data sprawl, unpatched systems and reporting gaps.

Four blind spots in the standard stack:

1. Compliance is not runtime resilience. 

A data protection officer, impact assessments and 72-hour breach notification meet the regulator's requirements, which carry fines of up to 2% of annual revenue. None of that patches a vulnerable system.

2. XDR watches behavior, not data sensitivity. 

When a stretched engineer copies a customer table to an unencrypted test server to hit a deadline, XDR sees what looks like routine admin activity. Without continuous Data Security Posture Management (DSPM), sensitive records sprawl outside protected perimeters.

3. Data in use is the gap. Bring-your-own-key encryption protects data at rest and in transit. To process a query, the application must decrypt the data in server memory, where privileged access on the host can reach it. Confidential computing (hardware-based trusted execution environments) narrows that exposure by isolating memory in hardware.

4. The human circuit breaker.
Detection tools fail when people stay quiet. Where teams fear blame or personal exposure under hierarchical reporting norms, anomalies get softened and logs sanitized to keep dashboards green, and leadership learns of a breach only when it surfaces externally.

The structural answer is four layers: regulatory governance, continuous attack validation (breach-and-attack simulation and external attack surface management), automated data discovery (DSPM), and hardware-enforced memory or edge isolation.

As January 2027 approaches: is your architecture built for runtime resilience, or just built to meet the checklist?

#Cybersecurity #DataSovereignty #IndonesiaTech #EnterpriseArchitecture

A Philippine flag, autumn leaves and a lot of laughter in Brittany 🇵🇭

Manila Water and our partner ESE-TECH Industrial Solutions were in France this week for the Factory Acceptance Test of SOFREL pressure data loggers for their network. They shared it with our friends from Indonesia, whose flag was flying on our pole that day 🇮🇩

We didn't just test a box. We tested the whole chain the utility will use every day:
📍 Data logger in the field
🔗 OPC UA server, an open standard
🖥️ LX SCADA in the control room

We ran forced and scheduled transmissions and checked every value and timestamp against the logger's own records. We also tested alarm call-in and acknowledgement, and cut the communication on purpose to check that missing data back-fills automatically.

Then we spent a morning at our LACROIX Symbiose electronics plant: SMT lines, 100% end-of-line testing, traceability.

A FAT is where trust is built. The utility's engineers ask the hard questions, our product and R&D teams answer on the spot, and everyone leaves with clear next steps.

Maraming salamat to the Manila Water team and to ESE-TECH for the trip and the partnership.

american companies outsource both manufacturing and white-collar service jobs globally—primarily to cut labour costs, access specialised talent and expand market reach, not to mention enjoy higher profits at home.

Key Destinations and Sectors

Manufacturing: China and parts of Asia have long been major hubs for electronics, apparel and industrial goods, driven by lower labour costs, supply chain scale and trade agreements.

IT, Software and BPO: India and the Philippines are top offshore hubs for software development, customer support and business process outsourcing (BPO), supported by large tech workforces and strong English proficiency.

Nearshoring: Countries like Mexico and Brazil attract US companies seeking closer time zones, bilingual talent and lower costs for software engineering, call centers and manufacturing.

Why It Happens & Current Shifts

Companies often pursue outsourcing for substantial cost savings (frequently cited at 50%–70% on labour), faster hiring and round-the-clock operations.

Then, Ultimate Stupidity Manifested (again)

On Nov 25, 2026, the don’s administration, via Office of the USTR, proposed new Sect 301 tariffs on 14 trading partners following an 8-month investigation into "excess industrial capacity" and subsidised production.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer stated that the levies target industrial subsidies, labour suppression and market-distorting practices that flood global markets with low-cost goods and undercut US manufacturing.

The 14 economies named include China, the EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, India, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Cambodia, Bangladesh, Singapore and Switzerland. Mexico and Norway were part of the probe but received no immediate decision.

China's embassy and commerce officials rejected the "overcapacity" premise as a pretext and warned of potential retaliation or WTO violations. The EU, Japan and Brazil have also pushed back against the accusations, while economists warn the new duties (what’s new?) could raise prices for US consumers.

What the fuck is this? Tariffs 3.0? US companies have already gotten their tariffs refunds. Booked them as bona fide profits instead of returning them to US consumers who paid for higher prices. Chumps.

The excess industrial capacity excuse is a pretty stupid reason to use when the US has been offshoring and nearshoring for decades. Decades. All was hunky dory back then when american firms were registering record profits.

Honestly, slap higher tariffs and prices will just go up again for american consumers. They’ll be the ones (again) paying out of pocket.

Have donny and rest of his pre-Jan 2027 GOP Senate and Congress not learnt from previous tariffs drawbacks? 

Play stupid games, win stupid prizes.

Seriously dumb mofos 🤣😂🥴🤭

Chips are getting rationed, answers are getting cheaper, and the effect is starting to show up in hiring. That is the thread through this week's newsletter. 

The Commerce Department closed a loophole that let Chinese labs rent advanced chips from data centers abroad, adding five countries to the license list, and one report says Moonshot AI promptly scrapped a roughly $150 million Blackwell rental in Indonesia. 

With supply tight, two labs launched on cost. OpenAI cut Astra's price and still met a cold reception, while Google's Gemini 4 Neon earned praise for answering differently than its rivals. 

Then Anthropic published interviews with 58 US companies. Only two had seen AI eliminate a job outright, but two-thirds said they were hiring less, and nine had cut contracted work, which is the corner of the market our industry lives in. 

The tech tip this week is a simple one: give your browser a boring chore, switch on approvals, and watch it work.

posts.text:
Hiring someone in Indonesia from abroad? You do not always need an Employer of Record.

There are three routes:

1. Pay them directly as an independent contractor. No local entity. Fits project or part-time work. Most teams pay through Wise, Deel or Payoneer.
2. Use an EoR. The provider holds the local employment contract and carries payroll, BPJS, THR and employee income tax, then invoices you. Fits a full-time employee when you do not want a local entity.
3. Set up your own company (PT PMA). The longest setup, but it fits a larger local team and a long-term commitment.

Two things that catch people out:
If a "contractor" relationship really works like employment, there is a misclassification risk.
Under Indonesian law the creator keeps rights to the work by default, so put an explicit IP-assignment clause in the contract.

Our guide compares the three side by side, with cost per role for 16 roles, from developers and data analysts to support and marketing. General information, not legal advice.

[Reading Indonesia: Democratizing Literature during "Efficiency"]

My second project as a student researcher.

Last semester, while working on research for Sociology in Literature and Popular Literature classes, I questioned the linguistic process of turning author's names into adjectives. 'Sadistic' referred to Sade's depiction of non-accidental pain, 'Kafkaesque' viewed sufferings as absurd. Both authors did not intend to publish their work.

A counterpart appeared in Indonesia by the end of 2023, where two shelves in our most trusted bookstore had been filled with works from Liye. Accusations aired from hiring ghost-writers, reserving slots on the shelves, and many more.

Then I realized, what we read has always been a part of democracy. If Kafka's friend obeyed his command, 'The Trial' and 'Metamorphosis' would have been ashes on the floor swept away during the World War. If readers did not respond to Liye's works, Indonesia might have never noticed the ghost-writing industry.

What we do as a country reflects the extension of democracy. However, has the political climate of Indonesia ever been adhering to literacy?

I do not think so. As per 2024 according to Badan Pusat Statistik, there was only 14 provinces (out of 38) with public libraries. The statistics for East Kalimantan alone stood with an average of 1 book per reader every month. And if we talk about human rights, women from Dayak Kenyah had lost their jobs of making traditional wooden weapons (called Sumpit) to deforestation. They needed to migrate to the city and readapt a whole life.

Why?

posts.text:
Every week I hear the same question from leaders in Indonesia: "We can't hire the AI talent we need. Can AI just do the work instead?"

My honest answer: partly.

Indonesia needs around 12 million digitally skilled workers by 2030 but has roughly 3 million. GenAI and agentic AI can stretch that scarce talent a long way. But only if we stop treating AI as a hiring substitute and start treating it as a redesign of work.

What I see leading procurement transformation:
• Time saved is not value created. Most people who save hours with AI get no guidance on what to do with them.
• Agents act on your data. Bad master data at scale means bad decisions at scale.
• The scarcest skill isn't prompting. It's people who know the process well enough to design, supervise and fix AI-enabled work.

AI doesn't remove the talent gap. If we're careless, it just moves it from doing the work to overseeing it.

I wrote more on this, including a five-step playbook, in my article below.
The question is no longer whether to adopt AI. It's whether your people are ready to lead it.

Where is your organisation getting stuck: tools, data, or people?

posts.text:
Four out of five private dollars in Southeast Asian tech now go to one kind of company.

The e-Conomy SEA 2026 report by Google, Temasek and Bain is titled "Building the intelligent economy". Its Bain analysis found that AI-focused companies captured about 80% of private funding in the region.

Why this matters for hiring:

Funding is a leading signal. When money moves to AI-focused companies, the teams around that work grow too. Not only machine learning engineers, but the people who make AI useful inside a business:

- Data engineers who keep the pipelines clean
- Cloud and DevOps engineers who run the infrastructure
- Business analysts who turn a use case into requirements
- Pre-sales and customer success people who explain the product to buyers

For hiring managers in Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand, it means competing for these profiles with well-funded teams. Clear role design and a fast, respectful process count for more than ever.

For IT professionals, it means skills that sit next to AI are worth building now, even if your title doesn't have "AI" in it.

At Base Camp we recruit across IT, go-to-market and corporate roles in Asia, and we see this shift in the briefs we receive.

Which role in your team has changed the most because of AI this year?

Read the report: https://lnkd.in/eKtTV92

As November closes and the season of gratitude settles in, I find myself reflecting on a question I am often asked by founders expanding into Southeast Asia:

After years in cross-border regulatory governance and luxury supply chain engineering, what is the only moat that truly endures?

Early in business, it is tempting to believe the answer is scale—more clients, larger headcount, faster turnover. Yet across ASEAN’s fragmented regulatory and climatic landscape, uncalibrated scale is often the first thing to break.
The only unshakable moat we have built at Solaris Vanguard andThe Packaging Lab (TPL) rests on two quiet pillars:

▫️1. Irreplaceable Institutional Trust:
When an international brand entrusts us with their ASEAN market access, they are not hiring a vendor; they are securing their sovereignty. By operating on a zero-commission model and locking product licenses inside an independent Custodian Notification Holder (CNH) vault, we give founders the freedom to scale across Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand without ever fearing distributor lock-in.

▫️ 2. Absolute Certainty in Physical Delivery:
Strategy means very little if a luxury box warps under 85% RH tropical humidity or leaks in maritime transit. Obsessing over 0.05mm pneumatic lid tolerances, flat-pack freight compression, and seamless secondary compliance labeling is how we turn promises into tangible retail authority.

Deeply grateful this month to the founders, manufacturing partners, and regional teams who share our refusal to cut corners. Scale can be copied; certainty cannot.

Wednesday taught the AI industry a lesson in one morning.

The Nasdaq fell 4.6%. Nvidia fell more than 9%. Anthropic touched $73.85 — 11% below its $83 IPO price.

By the close, almost all of it came back. The Nasdaq finished down just 0.6%. Nvidia closed at $149.30, down 3.9%. Anthropic closed at $82.79, up 1% — still below its IPO price.
Then, on Thursday, the harder news arrived. The Financial Times reported that Nvidia has told Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping AI servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, after new US export rules took effect on 19 November. It is not clear yet how long the halt lasts.
So the question is no longer only "how good is the model?"

It is also: can you get the hardware, can you prove where it will run, and can you ship a system that survives a rule changing overnight?
That is backend work. Deployment, compliance checks, audit trails, and systems that fail safely when the world changes around them.

I build those systems — Node.js, MongoDB, REST APIs, and agents that touch real inventory and real machines, with human approval where money moves.

If you are hiring a backend engineer who thinks about the whole system, not just the model, my inbox is open.
