posts.text:
A year ago, I started over. With experience.

I brought everything I have and learned so far. What I had to build was everything else.
And I didn't build it alone.

💕 The person beside me Jasmine Lee was there from day one. While I was out meeting people, she was quietly mapping most of the AV talent market. She picked up this industry faster than anyone I know, writes the sharpest profiles on our team, and shows up consistently, month after month. So much of what you see from me this year was built on work she did when nobody was watching.

This is what 2026 actually looked like.

🌱 The first half: going wide I said yes to almost everything. Every AV role including technical and regions we have never covered before. AI talent for a bank. An EVP for a global tech firm. A factory leader in China. A channel leader for cash technology. Midnight calls with US candidates. Two monthly challenge wins, in March and May.

Some of it worked. Some of it broke my heart. A candidate accepted an offer, then went silent. One search took four months to close.
But every yes showed me where I add the most value.

🎯 The second half: going deep AV became home. Building trust with search after search, until we helped build teams across APAC.
In June,Dessere Leong joined us. By July, the three of us who started recruitment together back in 2022 were sitting at an omakase counter as one team again.

Then the networking. The AVLIAS AGM, where one conversation became a new client and another made me the association's Talent Support & Recruitment Partner. Mumbai, where I kept bumping into familiar faces. Bangkok again, where industry leaders told me what they wished existed. CTS Connect Live, where clients pulled a recruiter into a room full of engineers.
In November, I spoke at PIFA for the first time. Then Jakarta, in my first kebaya, walking into a team I'd helped build.

📱 Finding my voice I started posting more honestly here. Not everyone liked it. When a message crossed a line, I spoke up. And this community grew to almost 10,000 of you.

What I didn't post about: The weeks I felt stretched thin. The days I am not sure if I was enough. Chasing payments. Holding my rates when giving in would have been easier. Walking away from business that didn't sit right with me. 

What the year taught me: Go wide to learn. Go deep to matter. Consistency beats intensity. Your values only count when they cost you something. Lead with trust, not fear. The more AI grows, the more human work matters.

To every client, candidate, teammate and stranger who became a friend this year: thank you. 

Jas, thank you for starting this with me.
Dess, thank you for coming onboard this train with us.

2027, I'm ready. 🌸

P.S. Photo by Jas, of course. She takes the best pictures of me. Beauty is in the eye of the beholder, and she's always seen the best in me. 📸

di rumah baguno balun.

An old Minangkabau pantun: go out into the world first, young man, because at home you are of no use yet.

For centuries, Minang men from West Sumatra have left their villages on merantau to seek wealth, knowledge and experience, and to come back better than they left. 

That tradition shaped Hatta, Agus Salim, Hamka and countless others.
It also shaped me.

I grew up in Padang, raised by my mother, in a house just 10 metres from the shoreline. 

Every morning I watched the fishermen come back from their night at sea, pulling their boats onto the sand with whatever the ocean had given them. Without knowing it, I was watching merantau in miniature: go out into the dark, work hard, and come home with something to share.

My mum can speak English and Dutch. Fluently. I learned English watching Scooby-Doo and Little House on the Prairie while she watched me practice. Then came Jakarta for university, and after that 35+ years in Oil & Gas across Indonesia, Singapore, the UAE, the US, Saudi Arabia and the UK.

One principle has stayed with me the whole way: "Alam takambang jadi guru", the wide world is your teacher.

But the rantau is only half of the story. 

As the Minang saying goes:

"Satinggi-tinggi tabang bangau,
baliaknyo ka kubangan juo."

However high the heron flies, it always returns to the pond it came from. 
Like those fishermen, we go out so that we can bring something back.

To every young engineer wondering whether to take the leap abroad: the rantau is waiting. 

Go, learn, and come home with your catch.

Pulau Pandan jauh di tengah,
di balik Pulau Angso Duo.
Hancua badan dikanduang tanah,
budi baiak dikana juo.

(The body returns to the earth, but good deeds are remembered.)

Greenfield sites are often misunderstood in infrastructure development.
Many assume an undeveloped site lacks readiness simply because legacy utility networks aren't already sitting inside the fence. From a civil and utility engineering perspective, the exact opposite is true at hyperscale.

Retrofitting fragmented brownfield plots means navigating undocumented subsurface pipes, fighting over congested right-of-way, and negotiating easements parcel by parcel.
On a contiguous ±350-hectare greenfield canvas along Greater Jakarta’s western corridor, you engineer from day zero: 
→ Dedicated underground ducting corridors for diverse dark-fiber routes and internal power spines
→ Direct frontage onto an ±8-meter provincial road built for 40-foot heavy container mobilization, paired with structured traffic impact governance (Andalalin)
→ Unified spatial separation across compute, captive clean energy, clean logistics, and water/utility buffers
→ Backed by 100% freehold (SHM) titles with unanimous landowner consent, upstream notarial-legal pre-audits aligned with local village leadership and BPN, and a single-window cash closing via mutually appointed PPAT/Notary

When you control the entire ±350-hectare geometry under a single-gate mandate, infrastructure stops being a patchwork, and becomes an engineered ecosystem.

For teams building hyperscale campuses in emerging markets: do you prefer retrofitting near legacy urban corridors, or engineering dedicated utility spines from a clean greenfield slate?

Seismic Design and 100-Year Flood Resilience for Data Center Campuses in Greater Jakarta: Mandatory Requirements for International Property Insurance

As hyperscale and AI data center campuses scale across Greater Jakarta and West Java (Bekasi, Cikarang, Karawang, and Bogor), physical climate and geotechnical risk underwriting has become a decisive gatekeeper for institutional project finance.

Positioned along the Pacific Ring of Fire and low-lying tropical river basins, Jabodetabek facilities face simultaneous exposure to high-intensity seismic activity and extreme monsoon flooding.

While sponsors frequently focus on grid capacity and fiber latency, international property insurers and debt-syndicate technical advisors increasingly reject or heavily surcharge campuses lacking rigorous structural and hydrological hardening.

From an energy investment origination and enterprise risk governance perspective, Greater Jakarta data center projects achieve institutional financial close only when site-specific probabilistic seismic engineering, 100-year-plus flood elevation defenses, and business-interruption insurance alignment are engineered upfront.

Six core pillars define institutional origination for seismic and flood-resilient data center campuses in Greater Jakarta:

 1. Site-Specific Probabilistic Seismic Hazard Assessment (PSHA): Going beyond baseline national building codes (SNI 1726) with site-specific geotechnical boreholes, deep-pile foundations, and soil-liquefaction mitigation protects structural integrity under severe earthquake scenarios.

 2. Base-Isolated Power, Cooling & Battery Hall Engineering: Installing seismic bracing and vibration-isolation mounts on high-voltage transformers, backup generators, chillers, and Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) prevents post-quake utility blackouts.

 3. 100-Year Flood Elevation & Hydrological Drainage Modeling: Elevating critical white-space floors, fuel tanks, and 150 kV substations well above 100-year (and 500-year) probable maximum flood lines—paired with dedicated retention ponds—eliminates water-ingress losses.

 4. Access-Road & Fuel-Resupply Flood Continuity: Verifying that primary and secondary logistics corridors remain passable during peak monsoon inundation ensures uninterrupted diesel/biofuel resupply and technician access.

 5. Property Damage & Business Interruption (PD/BI) Insurance Structuring: Engaging tier-one international reinsurance engineers during FEED secures bankable Probable Maximum Loss (PML) ratings, manageable deductibles, and comprehensive Delay-in-Start-Up (DSU) coverage.

 6. Clean Spatial Zoning (*KKPR*), Environmental Permits & ABAC Controls: Confirming watershed/drainage compliance under Persetujuan Lingkungan, unencumbered HGB land titles, and zero-tolerance anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABAC) governance protects institutional credit committees.

PP 33/2026 Sets a Floor, Not a Ceiling

BLUF: Compliance with Indonesia's PP 33/2026 is the floor of security, not the ceiling. The regulation mostly governs process: roles, assessments and notification. It does not, by itself, stop an attack.

With the regulation taking effect on 16 January 2027, many Jakarta enterprise security budgets are focused on compliance deliverables and standard XDR. Attackers do not read compliance binders. They exploit data sprawl, unpatched systems and reporting gaps.

Four blind spots in the standard stack:

1. Compliance is not runtime resilience. 

A data protection officer, impact assessments and 72-hour breach notification meet the regulator's requirements, which carry fines of up to 2% of annual revenue. None of that patches a vulnerable system.

2. XDR watches behavior, not data sensitivity. 

When a stretched engineer copies a customer table to an unencrypted test server to hit a deadline, XDR sees what looks like routine admin activity. Without continuous Data Security Posture Management (DSPM), sensitive records sprawl outside protected perimeters.

3. Data in use is the gap. Bring-your-own-key encryption protects data at rest and in transit. To process a query, the application must decrypt the data in server memory, where privileged access on the host can reach it. Confidential computing (hardware-based trusted execution environments) narrows that exposure by isolating memory in hardware.

4. The human circuit breaker.
Detection tools fail when people stay quiet. Where teams fear blame or personal exposure under hierarchical reporting norms, anomalies get softened and logs sanitized to keep dashboards green, and leadership learns of a breach only when it surfaces externally.

The structural answer is four layers: regulatory governance, continuous attack validation (breach-and-attack simulation and external attack surface management), automated data discovery (DSPM), and hardware-enforced memory or edge isolation.

As January 2027 approaches: is your architecture built for runtime resilience, or just built to meet the checklist?

posts.text:
Jakarta, Cairo, Lahore: same dollar salary dream, same next problem.

Kelvin Desman, a software engineer, wrote a guide on Medium for Indonesian developers chasing remote jobs paid in US dollars. His argument: skills are rarely the obstacle. Finding employers that hire from Indonesia and pay in dollars is. And dollar pay "holds its value even when the rupiah weakens."

I agree, and I'd add what comes after the offer letter. Four things I'd tell any developer in an emerging market:

1. Check they can pay your country. Not every payroll or contractor platform supports every country. Ask early.

2. Price the net, not the gross. Platform fees, transfer fees and the exchange spread come off the top.

3. Decide when you convert. Rent is local. Savings don't have to be. Convert what you spend.

4. Keep the paper trail. Contracts and invoices matter when your bank asks where the dollars came from.

The offer is step one. Getting paid is step two, in Jakarta, Cairo or Lahore.

Which one caught you out first: the fees, the timing or the paperwork?

Inspired by Kelvin Desman's piece on Medium, 6 Jul 2026

Why Global Data Center Developers Fail to Secure Land in West Java and Batam: The Fatal Mistake of Selecting Sites Without 150 kV Substation Capacity

As hyperscale cloud and AI operators accelerate expansion across Greater Jakarta, West Java (Bekasi, Cikarang, Karawang, and Purwakarta), and Batam, many international sponsors approach site selection through a traditional industrial real estate lens—prioritizing land price per square meter, highway access, and proximity to submarine cable landings.

Yet in Indonesia’s high-density power corridors, buying land before underwriting high-voltage (150 kV) substation headroom and transmission evacuation capacity is the single fastest path to stranded capital. 

Developing a 50–150+ MW AI campus requires dedicated high-voltage bay allocations, multi-year transformer lead times, and strict N-1/N-2 redundancy that local 20 kV distribution feeders simply cannot support.

From an energy investment origination and enterprise risk governance perspective, Indonesian data center land acquisitions achieve institutional financial close only when verified substation capacity, binding PLN Power Supply Agreements (PSAs), and clear transmission right-of-way (ROW) corridors are validated upfront.

Six core pillars define institutional origination for bankable powered-land selection in West Java and Batam:

 1. Substation Bay Headroom & Upstream Grid-Impact Verification: Confirming physical bay availability and transformer capacity at adjacent 150 kV (or 275 kV) substations—validated against PLN’s regional RUPTL grid expansion plan—prevents multi-year connection queues.

 2. Binding Phased Power Supply Agreements (PSAs) & Ramp-Up Schedules: Locking in contractual MW delivery milestones and connection-fee (BP/UJL) terms aligned with server-hall commissioning schedules protects project IRR.

 3. Dual-Feed Transmission Redundancy & Right-of-Way (ROW) Security: Securing diverse, unencumbered underground or overhead transmission corridors from two independent substations satisfies Uptime Tier III/IV and hyperscale resilience mandates.

 4. Integrated Spatial Zoning (KKPR), Flood & Water-Supply Underwriting: Verifying industrial zoning alignment, 100-year flood elevation defenses, and closed-loop water availability alongside power capacity eliminates sequential permitting roadblocks.

 5. 24/7 Clean-Energy & Behind-the-Meter BESS Integration Readiness: Assessing proximity to solar-BESS, geothermal, or Wilayah Usaha clean-power pathways ensures future compliance with global hyperscalers’ Scope 2 and 24/7 Carbon-Free Energy targets.

 6. Clean HGB Title Chain & Zero-Tolerance ABAC Controls: Conducting forensic land-title due diligence free of overlapping claims, paired with uncompromising anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABAC) governance across utility and zoning workflows, protects institutional credit committees.

The final training run of our Core ML model took 72 seconds. The game around it took 173 commits.

That was Challenge 4 at Apple Developer Academy @ UC, Jakarta. Five of us teamed up because we all wanted to go deep on AI/ML on Apple platforms.

We built Rosetta 2416. You're an astronaut stranded on a broken ship, and every repair task is a drawing. Think Among Us tasks, sketched with PencilKit.

So how did the model get made?

Create ML's image classifier. It reuses Apple's Vision feature extractor and trains a small classifier on top, so a run takes minutes and the model runs fully on-device.

3 versions in 4 days. Each one knew fewer objects, not more: 250, then 172, then 159.

The step that mattered most wasn't in Create ML at all.

A PencilKit drawing isn't a photo. We crop the strokes, pad them, flatten them onto a white 360x360 canvas, and only then hand it to the model. Now it sees what it was trained on.

A sketch passes if the model names the right object with at least 30% confidence. Forgiving on purpose. And when it still says no, there's a hint album.

Would you have set the bar higher than 30%?

The model war is over. The cost-per-task war just started.

GPT-6.2, Gemini 4 Neon and MAI Code 2 all shipped within days of each other. The interesting shift is not who is smartest — it is who is cheapest per coding task, and who decides which model runs.

For developers in Southeast Asia, this matters more than in Silicon Valley. Price sensitivity and local payment options decide adoption here, not benchmark scores. The winner will be the tool that is good enough, cheap enough, and easy enough to pay for in Jakarta, Ho Chi Minh City and Manila.

Applied Digital (Nasdaq: APLD) $5.4 billion Datacenter deal and Smart financing playbook lessons for#Indonesia

Applied Digital signed an 18-year agreement to build and lease a massive 150 MW AIDC to a major tech giant. Facility is scheduled to begin delivering computing capacity in H1 2028.

#Money: The tech giant will pay an average of 
$$300 million per year 
$$167 per KW per month
$$2 million per megawatt, totaling 
$$5.4 billion over the 18-year base term. 

If the tech giant exercises all its renewal options (extending the lease to 33 years), Applied Digital could earn up to $12.7 billion.

#Smart #Financing: Building a facility this big costs billions upfront. Instead of footing the entire bill alone, #AppliedDigital is using a 3-step funding strategy:

1. Putting in some of its own cash, ofcourse (balance sheet equity)

2. Tapping into a $5 billion funding partnership it already set up with a giant infrastructure investor,Macquarie Asset Management

3. Using the signed 18-year lease as a guarantee to borrow the rest from banks (#ProjectFinancing) at lower interest rates, since banks know a wealthy tech giant is locked into paying rent.

👉How This Model Can Be Replicated in Indonesia #Playbook

Indonesia is one of Southeast Asia's fastest-growing data center hubs ( #Batam, #GreaterJakarta #Bekasi #Karawang)

Local developers (such as DCI Indonesia ,NeutraDC /Telkom Indonesia SM+ or JV with regional playersDAMAC Digital)can replicate this exact playbook by combining 4 elements:

1. Lock in an #AnchorTenant First

Before pouring concrete, secure a 10-to-15+ year pre-lease with a global cloud provider (Amazon Web Services (AWS) Google Cloud Microsoft) or a major regional techfirm. A binding contract with a high-credit tenant removes the biggest risk for #lenders

2. Partner with Global Infrastructure Funds

Indonesian developers can form programmatic JV with global infrastructure investors / #SovereignWealthFunds (Indonesia Investment Authority (INA) GIC Brookfield ) to supply the heavy upfront equity needed for multi-hundred MW campuses

3. Non-Recourse Project Finance

With a long-term hyperscaler lease in hand, developers can raise project-level debt from banks (DBS Bank UOB SMBC Group , orPT Bank Mandiri (Persero) Tbk. backed strictly by the future rental cash flows rather than straining the#holdco

4. Solve Power & Land Bottlenecks

High-density AIDC require massive, uninterrupted electricity & requires securing dedicated HV substations from PLN Indonesia Power integrating renewable energy certificates#TRECs or captive#solar #geothermal power to meet green mandates & choosing strategic zones likeNongsa Digital Park for direct#SubseaCable access to#Singapore

5. For Grid Capacity and Transmission line upgrades

Team up with tech gaints & share the upfront capital required for upgrading/ reconductoring existing transmission lines. Apply #Google #Ohio cofunding model. Link in comments
